did.abstract: Dave Siglin was the Program Director at The Ark, a music club in Ann Arbor, Michigan. The collection includes the Ark's financial records and select correspondence; printed materials such as concert calendars, flyers, and posters; sound recordings; photographs of Ark performances; informal snapshots and publicity photos of performers. Also included are recordings of perfomances at The Ark, recorded by Siglin.

acqinfo.p: The papers were donated by Dave Siglin (donor no. 10045) in 2008; the digitized sound recordings were donated by Paul Conway on behalf of Dave Siglin in 2024.

bioghist.p: Dave Siglin served as Program Director for the Ark, an Ann Arbor music venue from 1968 until his retirement in March of 2008.

The Ark was established in 1965 as an outreach ministry--a coffeehouse--by five local churches: Northside Presbyterian Church, First Presbyterian Church, Calvary Presbyterian Church, Campus Chapel, and Presbyterian Campus Center. Though the Ark began as a partnership between religious organizations, the purpose of the Ark was not evangelism. Rather, the Ark founders wanted to provide university students with a safe, substance-free space where music, discussion and artistic expression could thrive, and a respite from the turbulent campus climate of the mid-1960s. The Ark's mission statement is as follows: "The Ark is a non-profit organization dedicated to the enrichment of the human spirit through the presentation, preservation and encouragement of folk, roots and ethnic music and related arts. The Ark provides a safe and welcoming atmosphere for all people to listen to, learn about, perform and share music."

Under Siglin's management, the Ark became a folk music institution, with many major folk artists of the 1960s-2000s performing at the Ark. Since its inception in 1965, the Ark has had three different homes: the first at the former Adams House at 1421 Hill Street. During the late 1970s, funding from the Ark's founding churches was discontinued and the Ark was reorganized as 501(3) non-profit organization; shortly after the reorganization, the Ark moved to its second site at 637 1/2 S. Main Street. The Ark opened at its current location at 316 S. Main Street in 1996.
The Ark continues to provide public music events as a non-profit organization. Anya Siglin, Dave and Linda Siglin's daughter, is currently the Ark's Program Director.

scopecontent.p: The Dave Siglin papers date from 1968-2008 and primarily document Siglin's management role at the Ark, an Ann Arbor music club. The papers have been arranged into five series: Administrative Records; Printed Materials; Photographs; Sound Recordings; and Digitized Ark Performances.

processinfo.p: The Sound Recording Series was previously described as a separate Dave Siglin Sound Recording Collection. It existed as a separate collection between 2012 and 2017. In 2017, the Dave Siglin Sound Recording Collection became a series within Dave Siglin Papers. In 2023, select materials from the Administrative Records series and from the Sound Recordings series were removed from the collection and returned to the Ark. As a result, Box 28-S and Oversize Volume 1 were eliminated.

scopecontent.p: Administrative Records contain the Ark's financial records and correspondence addressed to Dave and Linda Siglin. Financial records are part of this series and are most comprehensive for 1969 until the early 1970s, though scattered dates are represented in the collection. An oversized financial ledger also comprises part of this series.

odd.p: (Incoming correspondence to Dave and Linda Siglin)

scopecontent.p: Printed Materials contain monthly concert calendars from 1969-1982, bi-monthly event calendars from 1984-2008, concert flyers from 1969, 1972-1976, a news clipping file with various articles about the Ark, and miscellaneous printed matter. An outsized volume contains concert posters and flyers from 1978-1986.

scopecontent.p: Photographs contain images of performers and audiences during Ark concerts. Candid shots are included as well. There are two folders of photographs depicting Dave and Linda Siglin. Separate from photographs taken at the Ark are the publicity photos produced by performers' publicists and distributed for use in press and publicity materials. Photographs are arranged alphabetically. When the item contains the note "see also" this means that another image of that performer is contained among the images of another performer. The bulk of the photographs date from the early 1970s until the late 1980s.

scopecontent.p: The Digitized Ark Performances series consists of the digitized recordings from the Sound Recordings series, organized by format. Each recording is named for the featured performers and includes the original tape identification number. Many recordings include multiple performances across different dates; where possible, additional information was provided to identify each show.

The Ark featurs performances from a diverse range of communities. Highlights from this series include LGBTQ+ performers Louisa Jo "Lou" Killen, Lucie Blue, The Topp Twins, Heather Bishop, Casselberry and Dupree, Tret Fure, Cris Williamson, and Ferron (Ferron Foisy), among others. A number of Black folk singers and groups are also featured, including Odetta, Queen Ida, Elizabeth Cotten, Taj Mahal, Gaye Adegbalola, Saffire, and the Fairfield Four. Native American and First Nations performers include Joanne Shenandoah (Oneida), Farron (Metis), and Elisha Kilabuk and Koomook Nooveya (Iqalkuit).
